extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and reporters who write local and feature news
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting and writing miscellaneous local-news and entertaining feature stories (public institutions, business items, small human-interest incidents) emphasizing purpose, accuracy, and effective treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of miscellaneous local news
rubrics_metrics.description: Although most local events have been included in the various classes of stories discussed in preceding chapters, there remain several forms of city news that require separate consideration. Much interesting, timely information is to be found in schools, public libraries, museums, parks, and various departments of city government. Real estate, building, manufacturing, and business matters also furnish news of considerable interest and importance. Besides this information, there are many little incidents in the daily life of every city that have no significance as news but that can be written up as entertaining stories. Hotels, railroad stations, docks, and street cars are frequently the scenes of little comedies and tragedies... Animals no less than persons may be the central figures in these stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion defines the subject-matter inventory reporters should scan for miscellaneous local stories: public institutions, business/industry items, human-interest vignettes, transit/hotel/dock incidents, and animal-centered sketches. Treat each kind according to whether it is primarily informative (timely/significant) or entertaining (feature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of miscellaneous local stories
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim in one class of these local stories is to furnish timely, significant information in attractive form concerning public institutions and business activities. The purpose of the other class is to entertain the reader with little glimpses of the life of the city. Constructive journalism undertakes to stimulate the interest of every citizen in municipal affairs and in public institutions by putting prominently before him from time to time significant information about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the item is intended to inform (public-service/constructive journalism) or to entertain (feature sketch). For public-interest pieces emphasize significance and timeliness; for entertaining pieces emphasize human detail and readability while still serving civic interest when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The utmost accuracy in presenting information of public affairs and business matters, it is needless to say, is absolutely essential. It is important to maintain the same standard of truthfulness in writing entertaining feature stories, not because their contents are of vital importance, but because a newspaper, in order to command the confidence of its readers, cannot present anything in its news columns that is not true. Fictitious details are no more justifiable in feature stories than in news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify facts rigorously for both straight news and features. Never invent or embellish details; maintain the reader's trust as paramount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment — make stories attractive in form and style
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to interest the average reader in news of various municipal activities it is necessary to make the stories attractive in form and style. Striking facts and figures or unusual statements, featured at the beginning, catch the reader's eye and lead him to read the story as long as its subject matter and style interest him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with an attention-grabbing opener (striking fact, unusual statement, vivid image). Choose arrangements of material and style that keep the reader engaged while preserving accuracy and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statistics and comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective use of statistics and comparisons is shown in the story 'Public Schools Open'... Striking facts and figures or unusual statements, featured at the beginning, catch the reader's eye...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ well-chosen statistics and comparisons to dramatize scale or importance (but verify sources, provide context, and avoid misleading analogies). Use numbers to create a memorable lead when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devices for entertaining feature stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Since there is practically no news interest in entertaining feature stories, the reader's attention is attracted and held by the way in which the story is told. Narrative and descriptive beginnings, conversation, suspense, humor and other devices used in short stories and novels are well adapted to these news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For entertaining sketches borrow literary devices—narrative openings, descriptive scenes, reported conversation, suspense, and humor—but preserve factual accuracy. Use such techniques to make mundane incidents readable and engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hooking the reader with unusual openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Striking facts and figures or unusual statements, featured at the beginning, catch the reader's eye and lead him to read the story as long as its subject matter and style interest him. Effective use of statistics and comparisons is shown in the story 'Public Schools Open.' Two stories that begin with unusual statements are those entitled 'School for Backward Children' and 'New Feature in Manufacturing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select an opening that encapsulates the most dramatic or revealing element of the story (an unusual claim, vivid comparison, or startling statistic). Follow up immediately with substantiation and context to avoid hyperbole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading instruction — five points to observe
rubrics_metrics.description: Five points are to be especially observed: 1. Correct pronunciation of words at an acceptable rate of speed; 2. Expression of the meaning of what is read; 3. Distinct reading; 4. Pleasing use of the voice; 5. Ability to get the meaning of what is read silently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting on school programs or when describing pedagogical standards, use this explicit five-point checklist to evaluate or portray reading instruction; emphasize silent-reading development as formative of reasoning and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading tests / diagnostic procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure described for a reading clinic: collect teacher information about vision, hearing, breathing and attention; give progressively difficult prose, poetry and oratory selections; administer printed comprehension questions; have the pupil read printed stories and reproduce them; keep careful records of time and errors; project text on a screen while recording performance with phonograph, eye‑movement camera and chest-breathing instrument; use a shutter to measure how far beyond the stopped word the pupil can recall to determine area of attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a model diagnostic sequence for identifying causes of poor reading and crafting remedies: combine clinical measurement, progressive testing, reproduction/comprehension checks, and physiological/behavioral instrumentation to pinpoint deficits.

rubrics_metrics.name: School medical inspection — need for uniform methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The local board has been 'keeping tabs' on the doctors sent to the schools by the Board of Health. They have found little uniformity in the work; some visits lasting only a few minutes, and others a whole afternoon, while anywhere from nine to thirty pupils have been examined. As a result the local board has submitted a report ... suggesting that a more definite method of examination be required of the visiting physicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering school hygiene or medical-inspection programs, evaluate and report on procedural uniformity: require clarity on expected duration, number of pupils examined, whether physicians visit classrooms or only see referred children, and advocate standardized protocols (e.g., a department of school hygiene) where appropriate.
